summary: Discusses how network scanning changes in IPv6, where the huge default subnet size makes brute-force probing impractical. It explains that attackers can still find hosts by other means, and suggests address planning and management practices administrators can use as part of defence in depth. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 7707.

eli5.summary: Searching every house in a giant city is slow. But a burglar can still find homes by other tricks, so this paper shows how to hide yours better.

questions: why is ipv6 scanning harder than ipv4
how can ipv6 hosts be discovered
subtitle: Why scanning billions of IPv6 addresses is infeasible, and what to do instead

tldr.problem: IPv4 networks can be scanned with brute force because subnets have only 256 addresses. IPv6 subnets have 2^64 addresses, making brute-force scanning impractical.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents how attackers can discover IPv6 hosts through other means (DNS, routing info, logs, multicast) and suggests address allocation practices that raise the cost of finding targets.
tldr.outcome: Random host numbering is a low-cost defense layer, but security depends on defense-in-depth; randomness alone is not enough.

today: RFC 5157 is Informational and remains valid. It was replaced by RFC 7707, which updates the guidance with experience from IPv6 deployments and additional reconnaissance methods.

sections.title: Brute Force Scanning: IPv4 vs IPv6
sections.content:
IPv4 subnets typically have 8 bits of host address space, yielding 256 addresses per subnet. A remote attacker probing one address per second can scan an entire IPv4 subnet in under 5 minutes, allowing attackers to discover open services across many machines. IPv6 changes this equation: subnets have 64 bits of host address space by default, meaning 2^64 (over 18 quintillion) possible addresses. Scanning at one probe per second would take approximately 5 billion years, making traditional port scanning infeasible.

This fundamental shift prompted research into how IPv6 defenders can protect their networks. The RFC addresses both the apparent protection this provides and the reality that attackers can discover hosts through alternative methods.
sections.eli5: IPv4 has a small address space, so attackers can try every address fast. IPv6 is so huge that trying every address would take longer than the age of the universe. But attackers don't need to try every address when they can use other tricks.

sections.title: How Attackers Find IPv6 Hosts Without Scanning
sections.content: Attackers have several off-link methods to identify specific IPv6 addresses. They can learn the network prefix from public routing data and regional registries at /48 granularity. DNS entries for published services (MX relays, web servers) are readily scanned once discovered. Unrestricted DNS zone transfers reveal many internal addresses. Log files, archived email headers, and peer-to-peer application trackers all expose IPv6 addresses. Transition mechanisms like 6to4 and Teredo embed IPv4 addresses in IPv6 addresses, allowing predictable address generation. Multicast addresses can reveal unicast prefixes. If a single host is compromised, on-link methods like observing Neighbor Discovery traffic, probing multicast addresses, and inspecting the Neighbor Discovery cache quickly reveal other local hosts.
sections.eli5: If attackers can't guess your address, they steal your address book: they read web server names in DNS, inspect email headers in archived messages, watch what peers say in file-sharing apps, or spy on your network neighbors.

sections.title: Randomness in Address Allocation
sections.content: The simplest mitigation is random host numbering. Administrators should avoid sequential numbering schemes and should not allocate from [prefix]::1 upward. For stateless autoconfiguration hosts using the EUI-64 format, the host identifier includes the MAC address and 'fffe' stuffing, which reduces the search space to 48 bits if the vendor prefix is known. Avoiding predictable patterns increases attacker cost. Random allocation from DHCPv6 pools, starting far above the subnet base and with no sequential pattern, makes targeted discovery harder. Some operating systems support random interface identifier generation instead of embedding the MAC address, which further increases entropy.
sections.eli5: Don't number your hosts starting from one: mix them up randomly. It's just as cheap to be random as to be sequential, and randomness makes attackers' job harder.

sections.title: Limitations and Defense in Depth
sections.content: Address obscurity alone is not a security strategy; it is one layer in defense-in-depth. Dual-stack networks undermine IPv6 sparseness because hosts are still reachable via scannable IPv4. IPv6 privacy extensions (RFC 4941) provide temporary addresses that change over time, reducing the long-term value of harvested addresses, but administrators must understand the trade-offs with network management. Cryptographically generated addresses (CGAs) used with Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) increase the search space beyond stateless autoconfiguration. DNS, firewall rules, and routing controls are essential complementary measures. Administrators should coordinate between network and DNS teams to control what information is publicly exposed. These practices are low-cost compared to conventional sequential numbering and fit naturally into any deployment plan.
sections.eli5: Hiding your addresses helps, but that's just one lock on the door. You also need firewalls, careful DNS management, and the understanding that bad guys can still find you through other paths if they try hard enough.
